tasks.solution_overview: Reduce $\log_{4}x=\tfrac12\log_{2}x$ to obtain $\tfrac32\log_{2}x=6$, hence $\log_{2}x=4$ and $x=16$. At that root the summands are $4$ and $2$. The trial $x=64$ overshoots with sum $9$, and the two logs are not equal.

tasks.title: Parametric — compare log_a of letter powers against thresholds
tasks.context: Fix a base $a>1$ and letters $u,v>1$. Define $S=\log_{a}(u^{2}v)$ and $T=\log_{a}(u/v)$. Judge each claim as an identity in $a,u,v$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Expand $S$ by the product and power rules.

$$S=\log_{a}(u^{2}v)=\log_{a}(u^{2})+\log_{a}v=2\log_{a}u+\log_{a}v$$

The identity holds for every $a,u,v>1$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Expand $T$ and form the difference.

$$T=\log_{a}(u/v)=\log_{a}u-\log_{a}v$$

$$S-T=(2\log_{a}u+\log_{a}v)-(\log_{a}u-\log_{a}v)=\log_{a}u+2\log_{a}v$$

Equality with $3\log_{a}v$ for every triple would force $\log_{a}u=\log_{a}v$, which fails as soon as $u\neq v$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The same expansion $S-T=\log_{a}u+2\log_{a}v$ equals $3\log_{a}u$ for every triple only if $\log_{a}v=\log_{a}u$, i.e. only on the slice $u=v$, not universally.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Specialise to $u=v>1$.

$$S=2\log_{a}u+\log_{a}u=3\log_{a}u$$

$$T=\log_{a}(u/u)=\log_{a}1=0$$

Both claimed evaluations therefore hold on that slice.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

When $u=v>1$ one has $S=3\log_{a}u>0$ while $T=0$, so the two readings are unequal.

$$S\neq T$$

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: $S=2\log_{a}u+\log_{a}v$ and $S-T=\log_{a}u+2\log_{a}v$. Neither $3\log_{a}v$ nor $3\log_{a}u$ matches that difference for every triple. When $u=v$, one gets $S=3\log_{a}u$ and $T=0$, so $S\neq T$.

tasks.title: Invert a nested log equation log_2(log_3 x)=1
tasks.context: Solve $\log_{2}(\log_{3}x)=1$ on the natural domain where every intermediate argument is positive. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The natural domain of the left-hand side is $x>3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Apply the exponential of base $2$ to both sides of $\log_{2}(\log_{3}x)=1$.

$$\log_{3}x=2^{1}=2$$

That is exactly the forced inner level.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Solve $\log_{3}x=2$ by exponentiating with base $3$.

$$x=3^{2}=9$$

Uniqueness follows from bijectivity of $\log_{3}$ on $(0,\infty)$, intersected with the outer domain.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

At the trial $x=3$ the inner log equals $1$.

$$\log_{3}3=1,\qquad\log_{2}1=0\neq 1$$

So $x=3$ does not solve the nested equation.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The outer logarithm requires a positive argument, i.e. $\log_{3}x>0$.

$$\log_{3}x>0\iff x>3^{0}=1$$

The natural domain is therefore $x>1$, not the stricter cut $x>3$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

At $x=81=3^{4}$ the inner height is $4$.

$$\log_{3}81=4,\qquad\log_{2}4=2\neq 1$$

So $x=81$ overshoots the outer target.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Exponentiate once to get $\log_{3}x=2$, hence $x=9$. The natural domain of the left-hand side is $x>1$ (not $x>3$). The trials $x=3$ and $x=81$ fail the outer evaluation.

tasks.title: Hybrid — shifted log_2(x-2) with marked points
tasks.context: The figure shows $f(x)=\log_{2}(x-2)$ for $x>2$. Marks indicate exact evaluations. Combine the shift with base-two arithmetic. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Substitute the marked abscissa into the shifted rule.

$$f(6)=\log_{2}(6-2)=\log_{2}4$$

Since $4=2^{2}$, the height equals $2$.

$$f(6)=2$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The same shift at $x=4$ leaves a pure power of two.

$$f(4)=\log_{2}(4-2)=\log_{2}2=1$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Solve $\log_{2}(x-2)=3$ by exponentiating.

$$x-2=2^{3}=8\implies x=10$$

The candidate $x=8$ would require $x-2=6$, and $\log_{2}6\neq 3$, so $x=8$ is not a root.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The same exponential step produces the correct root.

$$x-2=8\implies x=10$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

At $x=3$ the shifted argument collapses to $1$.

$$f(3)=\log_{2}(3-2)=\log_{2}1=0$$

Since $0\neq 1$, the claim fails.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Shift then evaluate: $f(6)=\log_{2}4=2$, $f(4)=\log_{2}2=1$, and $f(3)=\log_{2}1=0$. Solving $f(x)=3$ yields $x-2=8$, hence $x=10$, not $x=8$.

tasks.title: Dense — when log equations are equivalent after a domain cut
tasks.context: Fix $a>1$. Compare the equation $\log_{a}(x-1)+\log_{a}(x+1)=\log_{a}(8)$ with the polynomial relation $(x-1)(x+1)=8$, paying attention to domains. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: On the domain $x>1$, the log equation is equivalent to $x^{2}-1=8$.
Every real root of $x^{2}-1=8$ solves the log equation.
The unique solution of the log equation on $x>1$ is $x=3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On $x>1$ both factors are positive, so the product rule applies.

$$\log_{a}(x-1)+\log_{a}(x+1)=\log_{a}\bigl((x-1)(x+1)\bigr)=\log_{a}(x^{2}-1)$$

Injectivity of $\log_{a}$ converts equality with $\log_{a}8$ into a polynomial relation.

$$x^{2}-1=8$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The polynomial $x^{2}=9$ has roots $\pm 3$, but only $x>1$ is admissible for the log equation.

At $x=-3$ the summand $\log_{a}(x-1)=\log_{a}(-4)$ is not real, so not every algebraic root solves the log equation.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Intersect $x^{2}=9$ with the domain cut.

$$\{x:x^{2}=9\}\cap(1,\infty)=\{3\}$$

Hence $x=3$ is the unique solution on $x>1$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Independently of the concrete base $a>1$, the product rule gives.

$$\log_{a}2+\log_{a}4=\log_{a}(2\cdot 4)=\log_{a}8$$

That is exactly the evaluation at $x=3$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The candidate $x=-3$ lies outside the domain $x>1$, so it cannot solve the log equation there.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: On $x>1$ consolidate to $x^{2}-1=8$. Domain rejects $x=-3$, leaving $x=3$. At that root the sum identity $\log_{a}2+\log_{a}4=\log_{a}8$ holds for every $a>1$.

tasks.title: Piecewise — match a log branch to an exponential branch at a knot
tasks.context: Define $p(x)=\log_{2}x$ for $x\ge 1$ and $p(x)=2^{x}-2$ for $0\le x<1$. Continuity at the knot is part of the analysis. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Compute the left-hand limit from the exponential branch.

$$\lim_{x\to 1^{-}}p(x)=\lim_{x\to 1^{-}}(2^{x}-2)=2^{1}-2=0$$

The right-hand value from the log branch agrees.

$$p(1)=\log_{2}1=0$$

Matching one-sided limits give continuity at the knot $x=1$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

On the log branch at the knot itself.

$$p(1)=\log_{2}1=0$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

At the left endpoint of the exponential branch.

$$p(0)=2^{0}-2=1-2=-1$$

So the claimed height $0$ is wrong.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Substitute $x=1/2$ into the exponential piece.

$$p(1/2)=2^{1/2}-2=\sqrt{2}-2$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

On the log branch at $x=4$.

$$p(4)=\log_{2}4=\log_{2}(2^{2})=2$$

Since $2\neq 3$, the claim fails.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: The two branches meet at height $0$ when $x=1$, so $p$ is continuous there with $p(1)=0$. Then $p(0)=-1$, $p(1/2)=\sqrt{2}-2$, and $p(4)=\log_{2}4=2$, not $3$.

tasks.title: Applied — half-life recovered by a logarithm
tasks.context: A mass follows $m(t)=m_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$ with $m_{0}>0$ and $\lambda>0$. The half-life $T$ is defined by $m(T)=m_{0}/2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Impose the half-life definition $m(T)=m_{0}/2$.

$$m_{0}e^{-\lambda T}=\frac{m_{0}}{2}\implies e^{-\lambda T}=\frac{1}{2}$$

Take the natural log and solve for $T$.

$$-\lambda T=\ln(1/2)=-\ln 2\implies T=\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

If one insists on common logs, change of base inserts an extra factor.

$$T=\frac{\log_{10}2}{\lambda\log_{10}e}$$

The displayed formula $\log_{10}2/\lambda$ omits that factor, so it is false.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Advance two half-lives from the initial mass.

$$m(2T)=m_{0}e^{-\lambda(2T)}=m_{0}(e^{-\lambda T})^{2}=m_{0}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{m_{0}}{4}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Divide the continuous path by $m_{0}$ and take the natural log.

$$\ln\frac{m(t)}{m_{0}}=\ln(e^{-\lambda t})=-\lambda t$$

The identity holds for every $t\ge 0$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The recovered formula $T=\ln 2/\lambda$ depends only on the decay constant, not on the initial mass $m_{0}$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Halving forces $e^{-\lambda T}=1/2$, hence $T=\ln 2/\lambda$, independent of $m_{0}$. Two half-lives quarter the mass. The log-linearisation $\ln(m/m_{0})=-\lambda t$ holds for all $t\ge 0$. Replacing $\ln$ by $\log_{10}$ without the change-of-base factor is incorrect.

tasks.title: Rebuild log_b from two exact table points
tasks.context: Assume $f(x)=\log_{b}x$ for an unknown $b>1$. It is known that $f(9)=2$ and $f(27)=3$. Rebuild $b$ and $f$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Translate $f(9)=2$ into an exponential equation.

$$b^{2}=9$$

With $b>1$ the unique solution is $b=3$.

$$b=3$$

Cross-check: $3^{3}=27$ matches the second seed $f(27)=3$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

With $b=3$, write $81$ as a pure power.

$$81=3^{4}\implies f(81)=\log_{3}(3^{4})=4$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Every logarithm vanishes at argument $1$.

$$f(1)=\log_{3}1=0$$

The claimed height $1$ is therefore wrong.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Rewrite the reciprocal as a negative power of three.

$$\frac{1}{3}=3^{-1}$$

$$f(1/3)=\log_{3}(3^{-1})=-1$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

If the base were $b=9$, the first seed would fail.

$$\log_{9}9=1\neq 2$$

So $b=9$ is incompatible with the table.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: The seed $f(9)=2$ with $b>1$ forces $b^{2}=9$, hence $b=3$; $f(27)=3$ confirms. Then $f(81)=4$, $f(1)=0$, and $f(1/3)=-1$. The rival base $b=9$ fails the seed.

tasks.title: Domain tangle — compound inequality with log_2(x-1)>2
tasks.context: Solve $\log_{2}(x-1)>2$ together with the natural domain $x-1>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The inequality is equivalent to $x-1>4$ on that domain.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The logarithm $\log_{2}(x-1)$ needs a positive argument.

$$x-1>0\implies x>1$$

That is the natural domain of the left-hand side.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Because the base $2>1$, the logarithm is strictly increasing, so inequality direction is preserved.

$$\log_{2}(x-1)>2\iff x-1>2^{2}=4$$

On the domain $x>1$ that equivalence is exact.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Simplify the inequality $x-1>4$.

$$x>5$$

Intersecting with $x>1$ leaves the same open ray, which is the solution set.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

At the boundary $x=5$ the logarithm meets the threshold exactly.

$$\log_{2}(5-1)=\log_{2}4=2$$

A strict inequality excludes its boundary, so $x=5$ is not a solution.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Substitute the trial $x=3$.

$$\log_{2}(3-1)=\log_{2}2=1$$

Since $1\not>2$, the point fails.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Domain $x>1$ plus the increasing map $\log_{2}$ turns $\log_{2}(x-1)>2$ into $x-1>4$, i.e. $x>5$. The endpoint $x=5$ and the trial $x=3$ fail the strict inequality.

tasks.title: Base-five logarithm — tick arithmetic past the marked base
tasks.context: The figure shows $f(x)=\log_{5}x$ with a mark at $x=25$. Use $f(5^{t})=t$ to judge the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write the marked abscissa as a square of the base.

$$25=5^{2}$$

$$f(25)=\log_{5}(5^{2})=2$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Continue one more power of five.

$$125=5^{3}\implies f(125)=\log_{5}(5^{3})=3$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The left side is immediate from the power rule.

$$f(5)+f(25)=1+2=3$$

The right side would equal $3$ only if $100=5^{3}=125$, which fails.

$$f(100)=\log_{5}100\neq 3$$

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Rewrite the reciprocal as a negative power.

$$\frac{1}{5}=5^{-1}\implies f(1/5)=\log_{5}(5^{-1})=-1$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Solve $f(x)=0$ by the defining property of logarithms.

$$\log_{5}x=0\iff x=5^{0}=1$$

The unique root is $x=1$, not $x=5$ (where $f(5)=1$).

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Powers of five give $f(25)=2$, $f(125)=3$, and $f(1/5)=-1$. The product check $f(5)+f(25)=3=f(125)\neq f(100)$. The unique root of $f$ is $x=1$, not $x=5$.

tasks.title: Table — recover base, then run a change-of-base chain
tasks.context: The table comes from $y=\log_{b}x$. Recover $b>1$, then evaluate the chain claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Translate $\log_{b}16=2$ into an exponential equation.

$$b^{2}=16$$

With $b>1$ the unique solution is $b=4$.

$$b=4$$

Cross-check: $4^{1}=4$ matches the first column.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Write $64$ as a cube in base $4$.

$$64=4^{3}\implies\log_{4}64=3$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The change-of-base chain telescopes through the middle base.

$$\log_{2}b\cdot\log_{b}8=\log_{2}8$$

The identity holds for the recovered $b=4$ (and indeed for every admissible middle base).

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Evaluate the telescoped value.

$$\log_{2}8=\log_{2}(2^{3})=3$$

Hence the product equals $3$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The recovered base is $4$. If $b=2$, then $\log_{2}16=4\neq 2$, contradicting the table.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: From $(16,2)$ recover $b^{2}=16$, hence $b=4$ since $b>1$. Then $\log_{4}64=3$, and the change-of-base chain $\log_{2}4\cdot\log_{4}8=\log_{2}8=3$. The rival base $b=2$ fails the table.

tasks.title: Quotient rule turns a two-log equation into a linear relation
tasks.context: Solve $\log_{2}(x+3)-\log_{2}x=2$ on the natural domain $x>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: On $x>0$ the equation is equivalent to $\dfrac{x+3}{x}=4$.
The value $x=-1$ is an admissible solution.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On $x>0$ both arguments of the original logs are positive (since $x+3>x>0$), so the quotient rule applies.

$$\log_{2}(x+3)-\log_{2}x=\log_{2}\frac{x+3}{x}$$

Exponentiate the level equation with base $2$.

$$\frac{x+3}{x}=2^{2}=4$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Clear the denominator of the reduced equation.

$$x+3=4x\implies 3=3x\implies x=1$$

The value $x=1$ lies in the domain $x>0$, and uniqueness follows from the linear relation.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Substitute the trial $x=3$.

$$\frac{3+3}{3}=2\neq 4$$

So $x=3$ is not a root.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

At the genuine root $x=1$ evaluate the first summand.

$$\log_{2}(1+3)=\log_{2}4=2$$

The claimed height $1$ is therefore wrong.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The natural domain requires $x>0$, so the negative candidate $x=-1$ is excluded before any substitution.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Consolidate to $(x+3)/x=4$, hence $x=1$. Trials $x=3$ and $x=-1$ fail. At the root, $\log_{2}(x+3)=\log_{2}4=2$, not $1$.

tasks.title: Parametric — competing logarithmic scales for the same letter argument
tasks.context: Fix $x>1$ and compare the two readings $A=\log_{2}x$ and $B=\log_{4}x$. Letters stay symbolic. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Express the base-$4$ reading through base $2$.

$$B=\log_{4}x=\frac{\log_{2}x}{2}=\frac{A}{2}$$

Rearrangement yields the exact scaling.

$$A=2B\qquad(x>1)$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

For $x>1$ the base-$2$ log is strictly positive.

$$A=\log_{2}x>0$$

Combined with $A=2B$ this forces $A>B$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Subtract using the scaling identity.

$$A-B=\log_{2}x-\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}x=\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}x$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Equality $A=B$ together with $A=2B$ would force $A=0$, i.e. $x=1$, which is excluded by the standing hypothesis $x>1$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Solve $A=4$ by exponentiating.

$$\log_{2}x=4\implies x=2^{4}=16$$

Then the companion reading is immediate.

$$B=\log_{4}16=\log_{4}(4^{2})=2$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Always $A=2B$ by change of base, so $A>B$ on $x>1$ with difference $\tfrac12\log_{2}x$. Equality $A=B$ would force $x=1$, excluded by $x>1$. The case $A=4$ recovers $x=16$ and $B=2$.

tasks.title: Double nested log_2(log_2 x) — domain and evaluation
tasks.context: Define $q(x)=\log_{2}(\log_{2}x)$. Every intermediate argument must be positive. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The outer logarithm requires a positive argument.

$$\log_{2}x>0\implies x>2^{0}=1$$

Together with $x>0$ from the inner log, the natural domain is $(1,\infty)$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Peel $16=2^{4}$.

$$q(16)=\log_{2}(\log_{2}16)=\log_{2}4=2$$

The claimed height $3$ is therefore wrong.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Peel $4=2^{2}$.

$$q(4)=\log_{2}(\log_{2}4)=\log_{2}2=1$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

At $x=2$ the inner log equals $1$.

$$q(2)=\log_{2}(\log_{2}2)=\log_{2}1=0$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

At $x=1$ the inner log vanishes.

$$\log_{2}1=0$$

The outer logarithm of $0$ is undefined, so $x=1$ lies outside the natural domain.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Domain is $x>1$ because the outer log needs $\log_{2}x>0$. Evaluations: $q(16)=2$, $q(4)=1$, $q(2)=0$. The endpoint $x=1$ makes the outer argument vanish, so it is excluded.

tasks.title: Hybrid — inverse pair 2^t and log_2 on one figure
tasks.context: The figure shows the inverse pair $y=2^{t}$ and $y=\log_{2}x$. Use inverse cancellation, not eyeballing. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The unique fixed point of $\log_{2}$ in $(0,\infty)$ is $x=2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Matched base cancellation removes the exponential.

$$\log_{2}(2^{5})=5$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The inverse cancellation removes the logarithm.

$$2^{\log_{2}7}=7$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Evaluate each cancellation separately for $t>0$.

$$\log_{2}(2^{t})=t,\qquad 2^{\log_{2}t}=t$$

Adding the two identities produces $2t$, not $t$.

$$t+t=2t\neq t\qquad(t>0)$$

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

A fixed point would solve $\log_{2}x=x$, equivalently $x=2^{x}$.

At the trial $x=2$ one has $\log_{2}2=1\neq 2$. For $0<x<1$ the log is negative while $x$ is positive. No positive fixed point exists.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Substitute the negative exponent $t=-3$.

$$\log_{2}(2^{-3})=\log_{2}(1/8)=-3$$

The cancellation identity holds at $t=-3$, so the claim that it fails is false.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Cancellation identities give $\log_{2}(2^{5})=5$ and $2^{\log_{2}7}=7$. The sum of the two cancellations is $2t$, not $t$. There is no fixed point of $\log_{2}$ on $(0,\infty)$, and $\log_{2}(2^{t})=t$ holds for negative $t$ as well.

tasks.title: Dense quantifiers — for every base and for some argument
tasks.context: Quantify carefully over bases $a>1$ and arguments $x>0$. A slip between 'for every' and 'for some' is fatal. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For every $a>1$, the map $x\mapsto\log_{a}x$ is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

By definition $a^{0}=1$ for every $a>1$.

$$\log_{a}1=0$$

The identity therefore holds for every such base.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Positivity of $\log_{a}x$ requires $x>1$. A concrete counter-example kills the universal claim.

$$a=2,\quad x=\tfrac12:\qquad\log_{2}\tfrac12=-1\not>0$$

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Existence needs only one witness.

$$a=2:\qquad\log_{2}\tfrac12=-1<0$$

So such a base exists.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

For $a>1$ the derivative of $\log_{a}$ is positive on $(0,\infty)$.

$$\frac{d}{dx}\log_{a}x=\frac{1}{x\ln a}>0$$

Hence the map is strictly increasing for every such base.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The power rule produces the coefficient $2$, not $1$.

$$\log_{a}a^{2}=2\log_{a}a=2\neq 1$$

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Every base $a>1$ satisfies $\log_{a}1=0$ and strict increase on $(0,\infty)$. Positivity of $\log_{a}x$ fails for $x<1$. Existence of a base with $\log_{a}(1/2)<0$ is immediate (e.g. $a=2$). Finally $\log_{a}a^{2}=2$, not $1$.

tasks.title: Piecewise — log of a squared expression versus twice the log
tasks.context: Compare $F(x)=\ln(x^{2})$ on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ with $G(x)=2\ln x$ on $(0,\infty)$ and with $H(x)=2\ln|x|$ on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Rewrite the square through an absolute value.

$$x^{2}=|x|^{2}\qquad(x\neq 0)$$

Take the natural log and apply the power rule.

$$F(x)=\ln(x^{2})=\ln(|x|^{2})=2\ln|x|=H(x)$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$G$ is only defined for $x>0$, while $F$ is defined for every $x\neq 0$.

On the negatives $F$ is finite (e.g. $F(-e)=2$) while $G$ does not even make sense, so $F=G$ fails on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Substitute $x=-e$ into $F$.

$$F(-e)=\ln((-e)^{2})=\ln(e^{2})=2$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The rule $G(x)=2\ln x$ requires a positive argument.

$$x=-e<0$$

Hence $G(-e)$ is undefined in $\mathbb{R}$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Evaluate $H$ at the same point.

$$H(-e)=2\ln|-e|=2\ln e=2$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Squaring forces $F=H=2\ln|x|$ on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$. The unsigned $G=2\ln x$ cannot match $F$ on the negatives. At $x=-e$ one has $F=H=2$ while $G$ is undefined.

tasks.title: Applied — pH as a common logarithm of concentration
tasks.context: Define $\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}[H^{+}]$ with concentration $[H^{+}]>0$ measured in the usual molar units. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $[H^{+}]$ drops by a factor of $10$, then pH rises by exactly $1$.
pH is a linear function of $[H^{+}]$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write the new concentration as $c/10$ and form the pH difference.

$$\Delta\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}\frac{c}{10}-\bigl(-\log_{10}c\bigr)=\log_{10}10$$

Since $\log_{10}10=1$, the pH rises by exactly one unit.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Substitute the concrete concentration into the definition.

$$\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}(10^{-3})=-(-3)=3$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The same evaluation produces $+3$, so the claimed value $-3$ simply drops the leading minus sign in the definition.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Compare pH at $2c$ with pH at $c$.

$$\Delta\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}(2c)-\bigl(-\log_{10}c\bigr)=-\log_{10}2$$

Doubling concentration therefore decreases pH by $\log_{10}2$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The map $c\mapsto-\log_{10}c$ is a composition of a logarithm with a sign change, which is nonlinear on $(0,\infty)$.

A linear rule would satisfy $\mathrm{pH}(2c)=2\,\mathrm{pH}(c)$, but $-\log_{10}(2c)=-\log_{10}2-\log_{10}c$ fails that test.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: A tenfold drop in concentration raises pH by $1$. At $[H^{+}]=10^{-3}$ one has $\mathrm{pH}=3$, not $-3$. Doubling concentration lowers pH by $\log_{10}2$. The dependence on concentration is logarithmic, not linear.

tasks.title: Rebuild a logarithm as the inverse of a given exponential
tasks.context: Let $E(t)=5^{t}$ for $t\in\mathbb{R}$. Let $L$ be the inverse function of $E$, defined on $(0,\infty)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

By definition the inverse of the exponential $E(t)=5^{t}$ is the base-$5$ logarithm.

$$L(x)=\log_{5}x\qquad(x>0)$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Write $25$ as a square of the base.

$$25=5^{2}\implies L(25)=\log_{5}(5^{2})=2$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Inverse cancellation along the exponential path returns the original time.

$$L(E(7))=L(5^{7})=7$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The other cancellation returns the original positive argument.

$$E(L(9))=5^{\log_{5}9}=9$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Rewrite the reciprocal as a negative power.

$$\frac{1}{5}=5^{-1}\implies L(1/5)=\log_{5}(5^{-1})=-1$$

The claimed height $1$ has the wrong sign.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: The inverse of $t\mapsto 5^{t}$ is $x\mapsto\log_{5}x$. Cancellation gives $L(E(7))=7$ and $E(L(9))=9$. Concrete values: $L(25)=2$ and $L(1/5)=-1$, so the rival height $1$ fails.

tasks.title: Domain tangle — product of logs requiring two inequalities
tasks.context: Consider $r(x)=\log_{2}x\cdot\log_{2}(x-4)$. Determine where $r$ is defined, then judge the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Each factor needs a positive argument.

$$x>0\qquad\text{and}\qquad x-4>0$$

The stricter cut is $x>4$, which is the natural domain of $r$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The test point $x=8$ satisfies $8>4$, so both $\log_{2}8$ and $\log_{2}4$ are defined.

$$8\in(4,\infty)$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

At $x=2$ the second argument is negative.

$$x-4=2-4=-2<0$$

Hence $\log_{2}(x-4)$ is undefined and $x=2$ lies outside the domain.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Evaluate each factor at $x=8$.

$$r(8)=\log_{2}8\cdot\log_{2}4=3\cdot 2=6$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

At $x=16$ the product is.

$$r(16)=\log_{2}16\cdot\log_{2}12=4\log_{2}12$$

Equality with $48$ would force $\log_{2}12=12$, i.e. $12=2^{12}$, which is absurd.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Domain forces $x>4$ because both $x>0$ and $x-4>0$ are required. Then $r(8)=3\cdot 2=6$, while $r(16)=4\log_{2}12\neq 48$. The trial $x=2$ makes $\log_{2}(x-4)$ undefined.

tasks.title: Graph — crossings of log_2 with the ray y=x/4
tasks.context: The figure shows $y=\log_{2}x$ and $y=x/4$. A crossing means $\log_{2}x=x/4$. Verify candidates by direct substitution. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Compare the two heights at $x=16$.

$$\log_{2}16=4,\qquad\frac{16}{4}=4$$

The common value $4$ means the curves cross at that abscissa.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The same substitution already showed both traces equal $4$ at $x=16$.

$$\log_{2}16=\frac{16}{4}=4$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

At $x=4$ the log height is $2$ while the ray sits at $1$.

$$\log_{2}4=2\neq 1=\frac{4}{4}$$

So $x=4$ is not a crossing.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

At $x=8$ the heights disagree.

$$\log_{2}8=3\neq 2=\frac{8}{4}$$

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

At $x=2$ the heights disagree.

$$\log_{2}2=1\neq\tfrac12=\frac{2}{4}$$

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Direct substitution: $x=16$ works because $\log_{2}16=16/4=4$. The candidates $x=2,4,8$ all fail the crossing condition $\log_{2}x=x/4$.

tasks.title: Table — recover ln-slope of an exponential path
tasks.context: An exponential path $y=y_{0}e^{kt}$ is sampled in the table. Work with differences of natural logs. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Along $y=y_{0}e^{kt}$ the log-level is affine in time.

$$\ln y(t)=\ln y_{0}+kt$$

The difference quotient between $t=1$ and $t=3$ therefore recovers the force.

$$\frac{\ln y(3)-\ln y(1)}{3-1}=k$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Insert the table heights.

$$\frac{\ln 20-\ln 5}{2}=\frac{\ln 4}{2}=\ln 2$$

So the continuous force equals $\ln 2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Form the ratio of the outer columns.

$$\frac{y(5)}{y(1)}=\frac{80}{5}=16$$

As a check, $e^{4\ln 2}=2^{4}=16$ matches the four-unit time gap.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The recovered force is $\ln 2\approx 0.693$, which is not equal to $1/2$.

$$\ln 2\neq\tfrac12$$

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Read the middle-left table entry directly.

$$\ln y(1)=\ln 5$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Log-differences recover $k=\ln 2$ from the columns $t=1$ and $t=3$. Then $y(5)/y(1)=16$, while $k\neq 1/2$. Also $\ln y(1)=\ln 5$ matches the table directly.

tasks.title: Symbolic — evaluate a three-factor change-of-base chain
tasks.context: Simplify the product $P=\log_{2}3\cdot\log_{3}5\cdot\log_{5}4$ by telescoping, then judge the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Expand every factor through natural logs and cancel.

$$P=\frac{\ln 3}{\ln 2}\cdot\frac{\ln 5}{\ln 3}\cdot\frac{\ln 4}{\ln 5}=\frac{\ln 4}{\ln 2}=\log_{2}4$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Evaluate the telescoped logarithm.

$$\log_{2}4=\log_{2}(2^{2})=2$$

Hence $P=2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Collapse the last two factors first.

$$\log_{3}5\cdot\log_{5}4=\log_{3}4$$

Multiplying by the remaining front factor yields the two-factor form.

$$P=\log_{2}3\cdot\log_{3}4$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The telescoping value is $2$, so the rival claim $P=3$ fails.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Compare the telescoped value with $\log_{5}2$.

$$P=2\neq\log_{5}2$$

because $5^{2}=25\neq 2$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: The three-factor chain telescopes to $\log_{2}4=2$. Intermediate collapse also gives $\log_{2}3\cdot\log_{3}4$. The rivals $3$ and $\log_{5}2$ fail.

tasks.title: Parametric — solve a^{2t}=c^3 for the unknown exponent
tasks.context: Fix $a>1$ and $c>0$. Solve $a^{2t}=c^{3}$ for the real unknown $t$, expressing the answer through logarithms. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Take $\log_{a}$ of both sides of $a^{2t}=c^{3}$.

$$2t=\log_{a}(c^{3})=3\log_{a}c$$

Solve for the unknown exponent.

$$t=\frac{3\log_{a}c}{2}$$

Uniqueness follows from injectivity of the exponential in the base $a>1$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Change of base replaces $\log_{a}c$ by a quotient of natural logs.

$$\log_{a}c=\frac{\ln c}{\ln a}\implies t=\frac{3\ln c}{2\ln a}$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

If $c=a$, then $\log_{a}c=1$, so $t=3/2$, not $3$.

$$t=\frac{3\cdot 1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}\neq 3$$

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The same specialisation produces the correct half-integer.

$$t=\frac{3}{2}$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

If $c=1$, then $\log_{a}1=0$, so the exponent vanishes.

$$t=\frac{3\cdot 0}{2}=0\neq 1$$

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Logging both sides yields $2t=3\log_{a}c$, hence $t=3\log_{a}c/2=3\ln c/(2\ln a)$. When $c=a$ one gets $t=3/2$; when $c=1$ one gets $t=0$.

tasks.title: Nested — peel 2^{log_2(log_2(16))} and mismatched bases
tasks.context: Evaluate nested compositions that mix exponentials and logarithms, including mismatched bases. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Innermost: $\log_{2}16=4$. The outer exponential then cancels against $\log_{2}$.

$$2^{\log_{2}(\log_{2}16)}=2^{\log_{2}4}=4$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The same peel yields $4$, so the claimed value $2$ is wrong.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Write the mismatched base $10$ as a power of $2$.

$$10=2^{\log_{2}10}$$

Raise both sides to the power $\log_{2}16=4$.

$$10^{\log_{2}16}=(2^{\log_{2}10})^{4}=2^{4\log_{2}10}$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Matched cancellation removes the outer exponential.

$$\log_{2}\bigl(2^{\log_{2}3+\log_{2}5}\bigr)=\log_{2}3+\log_{2}5$$

The sum of logs is the log of the product.

$$\log_{2}3+\log_{2}5=\log_{2}15$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Combine the exponents inside the exponential.

$$e^{\ln 3+\ln 4}=e^{\ln 12}=12$$

Since $12\neq 7$, the claim fails.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Peeling $2^{\log_{2}(\log_{2}16)}$ gives $4$. Rewriting $10$ in base $2$ produces $2^{4\log_{2}10}$. Matched cancellation yields $\log_{2}15$, while $e^{\ln 3+\ln 4}=12$, not $7$.

tasks.title: Hybrid — natural log figure with e-mark arithmetic
tasks.context: The figure shows $f(x)=\ln x$ with a mark at $x=e$. Use $\ln(e^{t})=t$ and change of base. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Cancel the exponential against the natural log.

$$f(e^{2})=\ln(e^{2})=2$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The natural log vanishes at argument $1$.

$$f(1)=\ln 1=0$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Evaluate numerator and denominator separately.

$$f(e^{3})=\ln(e^{3})=3,\qquad f(e)=1$$

The quotient is therefore exactly $3$.

$$\frac{f(e^{3})}{f(e)}=3$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Change of base converts the ratio of natural logs into a base-$2$ log.

$$\frac{f(8)}{f(2)}=\frac{\ln 8}{\ln 2}=\log_{2}8$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Rewrite the reciprocal as a negative power of $e$.

$$f(1/e)=\ln(e^{-1})=-1$$

The claimed height $1$ has the wrong sign.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Natural-log evaluations: $f(e^{2})=2$, $f(1)=0$, and $f(1/e)=-1$. The ratio $f(e^{3})/f(e)=3$, and $f(8)/f(2)$ recovers $\log_{2}8$ by change of base.

tasks.title: Dense — precisely when a logarithmic inequality holds
tasks.context: Fix $a>1$. Characterise precisely when $\log_{a}x>\log_{a}y$ for $x,y>0$, and related variants. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

For every base $a>1$ the logarithm is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.

$$x>y>0\iff\log_{a}x>\log_{a}y$$

That is precisely the claimed biconditional.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The reversed characterisation $x<y$ would fit a base in $(0,1)$, where the logarithm is decreasing.

For $a>1$ the order is preserved, not reversed, so the claim fails.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Arguments below $1$ produce negative logs, while arguments above $1$ produce positive logs.

$$0<x<1<y\implies\log_{a}x<0<\log_{a}y$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

By definition $a^{0}=1$, so the log vanishes exactly at $1$.

$$\log_{a}x=0\iff x=1$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The level equation $\log_{a}x=1$ forces $x=a$, not $x=0$.

$$\log_{a}x=1\iff x=a\neq 0$$

Moreover $x=0$ is not even in the domain.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: For $a>1$, logs preserve order, vanish only at $1$, and equal $1$ only at $a$. Arguments below $1$ give negative logs, so the reversed inequality characterisation fits bases in $(0,1)$, not $a>1$.

tasks.title: Piecewise — log_2 of |x-3| and the split domain
tasks.context: Define $s(x)=\log_{2}|x-3|$ for $x\neq 3$. Split into $x>3$ and $x<3$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On the half-line $x>3$ the expression inside the absolute value is already positive.

$$|x-3|=x-3\qquad(x>3)$$

Taking $\log_{2}$ yields the claimed branch.

$$s(x)=\log_{2}(x-3)$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

On the complementary half-line $x<3$ the absolute value flips the sign.

$$|x-3|=3-x\qquad(x<3)$$

$$s(x)=\log_{2}(3-x)$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

At $x=7>3$ use the right-hand branch.

$$s(7)=\log_{2}(7-3)=\log_{2}4=2$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

At $x=-1<3$ use the left-hand branch.

$$s(-1)=\log_{2}(3-(-1))=\log_{2}4=2$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

At $x=3$ the argument of the logarithm vanishes.

$$|3-3|=0$$

Since $\log_{2}0$ is undefined, $s(3)$ does not exist and cannot equal $0$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Absolute value splits into $\log_{2}(x-3)$ for $x>3$ and $\log_{2}(3-x)$ for $x<3$. Both $x=7$ and $x=-1$ give $s=2$, while $x=3$ makes the argument vanish and is excluded.

tasks.title: Applied — Richter-style magnitude as a logarithm of amplitude
tasks.context: A magnitude is modelled by $M=\log_{10}(A/A_{0})$ with amplitude $A>0$ and reference $A_{0}>0$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $A$ grows by a factor of $1000$, then $M$ increases by $3$.
If $A$ grows by a factor of $2$, then $M$ increases by $2$.
If $A$ and $A_{0}$ are both multiplied by $10$, then $M$ increases by $1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Raising amplitude by a factor of $1000$ changes the magnitude by a pure common logarithm.

$$\Delta M=\log_{10}\frac{1000A}{A}=\log_{10}1000$$

Since $1000=10^{3}$, the increment is exactly $3$.

$$\Delta M=3$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The same difference with factor $2$ produces.

$$\Delta M=\log_{10}2$$

Because $\log_{10}2\neq 2$, the claim fails.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Expand the two magnitudes and cancel the common reference.

$$M(A)-M(B)=\log_{10}\frac{A}{A_{0}}-\log_{10}\frac{B}{A_{0}}=\log_{10}\frac{A}{B}$$

The difference is independent of $A_{0}$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

When amplitude equals the reference, the argument of the log is $1$.

$$M=\log_{10}\frac{A_{0}}{A_{0}}=\log_{10}1=0$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Scale both $A$ and $A_{0}$ by the same factor $10$.

$$M_{\mathrm{new}}=\log_{10}\frac{10A}{10A_{0}}=\log_{10}\frac{A}{A_{0}}=M$$

The magnitude is unchanged, so it does not increase by $1$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: A thousandfold amplitude jump adds $3$ to $M$; a twofold jump adds $\log_{10}2\neq 2$. Differences cancel $A_{0}$. Simultaneous scaling of $A$ and $A_{0}$ by $10$ leaves the ratio — and hence $M$ — fixed.

tasks.title: Rebuild — continuous log-like map from a seed and the power rule
tasks.context: Suppose $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfies $f(x^{2})=2f(x)$ for every $x>0$, is continuous, and $f(8)=3$. Assume also $f$ is of the form $c\log_{2}$ (the continuous solutions of the power relation). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Under the standing form $f=c\log_{2}$, feed in the seed.

$$f(8)=c\log_{2}8=c\cdot 3=3$$

Solve for the scalar.

$$c=1$$

Hence $f(x)=\log_{2}x$ for every $x>0$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

With $c=1$, evaluate at $x=64=2^{6}$.

$$f(64)=\log_{2}(2^{6})=6$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

At the pure base argument the log equals $1$.

$$f(2)=\log_{2}2=1$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Rewrite the reciprocal as a negative power.

$$\frac{1}{8}=2^{-3}\implies f(1/8)=\log_{2}(2^{-3})=-3$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

At $x=4=2^{2}$ the rebuilt rule gives $2$, not $4$.

$$f(4)=\log_{2}4=2\neq 4$$

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: The seed $f(8)=3$ forces $c\log_{2}8=3c=3$, hence $c=1$ and $f=\log_{2}$. Then $f(64)=6$, $f(2)=1$, $f(1/8)=-3$, while $f(4)=2\neq 4$.

tasks.title: Domain tangle — inequality for a nested logarithm
tasks.context: Solve $\log_{2}(\log_{3}x)>1$ on the natural domain of the nested logarithm. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The inequality is equivalent to $\log_{3}x>2$ on that domain.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The outer logarithm needs a positive argument, i.e. $\log_{3}x>0$.

$$\log_{3}x>0\iff x>3^{0}=1$$

That is the natural domain of the nested left-hand side.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Because the outer base $2>1$, the inequality $\log_{2}(\cdot)>1$ is equivalent to the argument exceeding $2$.

$$\log_{2}(\log_{3}x)>1\iff\log_{3}x>2^{1}=2$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Solve $\log_{3}x>2$ by exponentiating with base $3$.

$$x>3^{2}=9$$

Intersecting with the domain $x>1$ leaves the open ray $x>9$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

At the boundary $x=9$ the outer log meets the threshold exactly.

$$\log_{2}(\log_{3}9)=\log_{2}2=1$$

A strict inequality excludes its boundary, so $x=9$ is not a solution.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

At the trial $x=3$ the inner log equals $1$.

$$\log_{2}(\log_{3}3)=\log_{2}1=0\not>1$$

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Domain $x>1$ plus $\log_{3}x>2$ yields $x>9$. The endpoint $x=9$ gives outer value $1$, and the trial $x=3$ gives outer value $0$, so both fail the strict inequality.

tasks.title: Graph log_2 — multi-step product and quotient checks
tasks.context: Again $f(x)=\log_{2}x$ on the figure. Each claim needs a calculation with at least two evaluations. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The difference of logs is the log of the quotient.

$$f(24)-f(3)=\log_{2}\frac{24}{3}=\log_{2}8$$

Since $\log_{2}8=f(8)$, the claimed identity holds.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The same quotient already equals $\log_{2}8$.

$$\log_{2}8=3$$

Hence $f(24)-f(3)=3$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The sum of logs is the log of the product.

$$f(9)+f(4)=\log_{2}(9\cdot 4)=\log_{2}36=f(36)$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The sum equals $f(36)$, and $36\neq 13$, so the sum cannot equal $f(13)$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The power rule doubles the log.

$$2f(8)=2\log_{2}8=\log_{2}(8^{2})=\log_{2}64=f(64)$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Quotient and product rules give $f(24)-f(3)=f(8)=3$ and $f(9)+f(4)=f(36)$. Also $2f(8)=f(64)$. The rival $f(13)$ fails because $9\cdot 4=36\neq 13$.

tasks.title: Table — base-three logs with a false extrapolation
tasks.context: The table lists exact values of $\log_{3}x$. Use them to judge extrapolations. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $81$ as a pure power of three.

$$81=3^{4}\implies\log_{3}81=4$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Rewrite the reciprocal as a negative power.

$$\frac{1}{27}=3^{-3}\implies\log_{3}(1/27)=-3$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Factor $6=2\cdot 3$ and apply the product rule.

$$\log_{3}6=\log_{3}(2\cdot 3)=\log_{3}2+\log_{3}3=\log_{3}2+1$$

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

If $\log_{3}6=2$, exponentiating would force $6=3^{2}=9$.

$$6\neq 9$$

So the extrapolation to height $2$ fails.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The difference of logs is the log of the quotient.

$$\log_{3}9-\log_{3}3=\log_{3}\frac{9}{3}=\log_{3}3=1$$

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: Powers of three give $\log_{3}81=4$ and $\log_{3}(1/27)=-3$. The product rule writes $\log_{3}6=\log_{3}2+1\neq 2$. Also $\log_{3}9-\log_{3}3=1$.

tasks.title: Symbolic — ln equation that becomes a quadratic after exp
tasks.context: Solve $\ln(x)+\ln(x-3)=\ln(4x)$ on the natural domain $x>3$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: On $x>3$ the equation is equivalent to $x(x-3)=4x$.
After cancelling the factor $x>0$, one obtains $x-3=4$.
The unique solution in the domain is $x=7$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

On $x>3$ both $x$ and $x-3$ are positive, so the product rule applies.

$$\ln x+\ln(x-3)=\ln\bigl(x(x-3)\bigr)$$

Injectivity of $\ln$ converts equality with $\ln(4x)$ into a polynomial relation.

$$x(x-3)=4x$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

On the domain $x>3$ one may divide by the positive factor $x$.

$$x-3=4$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Solve the reduced linear equation.

$$x=7$$

Since $7>3$, the root lies in the natural domain, and uniqueness follows from the linear reduction.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

At $x=0$ every logarithm in the original equation is undefined, so $x=0$ is not admissible.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Substitute the trial $x=4$ into the polynomial form.

$$4(4-3)=4,\qquad 4\cdot 4=16$$

Since $4\neq 16$, the point $x=4$ is not a root.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Consolidate to $x(x-3)=4x$. On $x>3$ cancel the positive factor $x$ to get $x-3=4$, hence $x=7$. The trials $x=0$ and $x=4$ fail.

tasks.title: Parametric — unknown base recovered from one letter equation
tasks.context: Suppose $b>1$ satisfies $\log_{b}(b^{3}\cdot 4)=5$. Recover $b$, then judge the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Expand the left-hand side by the product rule.

$$\log_{b}(b^{3}\cdot 4)=\log_{b}(b^{3})+\log_{b}4=3+\log_{b}4$$

The seed equation becomes $3+\log_{b}4=5$, so $\log_{b}4=2$, hence $b^{2}=4$.

$$b=2\qquad(b>1)$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

With the recovered base, evaluate directly.

$$\log_{2}4=\log_{2}(2^{2})=2$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

If $b=4$, the seed fails.

$$3+\log_{4}4=3+1=4\neq 5$$

So $b=4$ is incompatible.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

With $b=2$, write $32$ as a pure power.

$$\log_{2}32=\log_{2}(2^{5})=5$$

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

At $x=8$ the height is $3$, not $4$.

$$\log_{2}8=\log_{2}(2^{3})=3\neq 4$$

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: From $3+\log_{b}4=5$ recover $\log_{b}4=2$, hence $b^{2}=4$ and $b=2$ since $b>1$. Then $\log_{2}32=5$ while $\log_{2}8=3$. The rival base $b=4$ fails the seed equation.

tasks.title: Nested peel — solve log_2(log_2(log_2 x))=1
tasks.context: Solve $\log_{2}\bigl(\log_{2}(\log_{2}x)\bigr)=1$ on the natural domain of the triple nesting. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Apply the exponential of base $2$ to both sides.

$$\log_{2}(\log_{2}x)=2^{1}=2$$

That is the forced middle level.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Apply the exponential once more.

$$\log_{2}x=2^{2}=4$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Exponentiate a third time to recover the argument.

$$x=2^{4}=16$$

Uniqueness follows from bijectivity of each successive logarithm on its range.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Peel the giant candidate $65536=2^{16}$.

$$\log_{2}65536=16,\quad\log_{2}16=4,\quad\log_{2}4=2$$

The outer value is $2$, not $1$, so $x=65536$ is not a root.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The input $x=2^{16}$ is identical to $65536$, so the same peel applies and again yields outer value $2$, not $1$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Peeling once gives $\log_{2}(\log_{2}x)=2$, twice gives $\log_{2}x=4$, hence $x=16$. The giant $2^{16}=65536$ peels to outer value $2$, not $1$.

tasks.title: Hybrid — piecewise hit, path-average force, and two false clocks
tasks.context: A fund starts at $A=1024$, grows at continuous force $\alpha=\ln 2/8$ until $t=\tau$ with $\alpha\tau=\ln 2$, then at force $\beta=\ln 2/16$. Target level $M=4A$. The figure shows the path. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The target is reached strictly after the rate switch, at $t_{\mathrm{hit}}=\tau+\ln 2/\beta$.
The hitting time equals $\ln(M/A)/\alpha$ (constant early force, no switch).
At the switch the fund already meets or exceeds $M$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Chain the segments and solve $f(t)=M$ in the late regime.

$$f(\tau)=A e^{\alpha\tau}=2A$$

$$t_{\mathrm{hit}}=\tau+\frac{\ln(M/(2A))}{\beta}=\tau+\frac{\ln 2}{\beta}=24$$

$$24>\tau=8$$

The hit sits strictly after the switch at the claimed clock.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Average force is total log-increment per unit time.

$$\bar k=\frac{\ln(M/A)}{t_{\mathrm{hit}}}=\frac{\ln 4}{24}=0.057762$$

$$A e^{\bar k\,t_{\mathrm{hit}}}=4096$$

The average force recovers the target exactly.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A constant-$\alpha$ formula pretends the switch never happened.

$$t_{\alpha}=\frac{\ln(M/A)}{\alpha}=\frac{\ln 4}{\alpha}=16$$

$$t_{\mathrm{hit}}=24\neq16$$

The no-switch clock is not the piecewise hitting time.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Change-of-base alone does not cancel the early segment.

$$\frac{\log_2(M/A)}{\beta}=\frac{2}{\beta}=46.1662$$

$$t_{\mathrm{hit}}=24\neq46.1662$$

Dividing $\log_2(M/A)$ by $\beta$ skips the early force entirely.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Evaluate the level at the kink.

$$f(\tau)=2A=2048,\qquad M=4A=4096$$

At the switch the fund is still strictly below the target.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: With $\alpha\tau=\ln 2$, $f(\tau)=2A$. Target $M=4A$ forces $t_{\mathrm{hit}}=\tau+\ln 2/\beta=24$. Path-average $\bar k=\ln(M/A)/t_{\mathrm{hit}}=0.057762$. Constant-$\alpha$ mis-clock $t_\alpha=16$; mis-scaled change-of-base $\log_2(M/A)/\beta=46.1662$.

tasks.title: Graph — crossing populations, log-gap, and a flipped meeting formula
tasks.context: Two populations follow $A(t)=A_0 e^{k_A t}$ and $B(t)=B_0 e^{k_B t}$ with $A_0=800$, $k_A=0.04$, $B_0=1200$, $k_B=0.01$. The figure shows both paths on $[0,50]$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The populations meet at some time strictly inside $(0,50)$.
The meeting time equals the doubling time of $A$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Set $A_0 e^{k_A t}=B_0 e^{k_B t}$ and take logs.

$$t^*=\frac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{k_A-k_B}\approx13.5155$$

$$0<13.5155<50$$

A unique crossing sits inside the open interval.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Evaluate both levels at the horizon.

$$A(50)\approx5911.2449,\qquad B(50)\approx1978.4655$$

Population $A$ is strictly larger at the horizon.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Log-quotient is affine in $t$.

$$\ln\frac{A(t)}{B(t)}=\ln\frac{A_0}{B_0}+(k_A-k_B)t$$

$$\ln\frac{A(50)}{B(50)}\approx1.0945$$

The log-gap identity holds at the horizon.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The correct ratio is $B_0/A_0$, not $A_0/B_0$.

$$\frac{\ln(A_0/B_0)}{k_A-k_B}\approx-13.5155$$

$$t^*\approx13.5155$$

Flipping the ratio flips the sign of the meeting time.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Doubling of $A$ solves $e^{k_A t}=2$, unrelated to the cross.

$$t_{\times 2}=\frac{\ln 2}{k_A}\approx17.3287$$

$$t^*\approx13.5155\neq17.3287$$

Doubling time of $A$ is not the meeting clock.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: $A(t)=800e^{0.04t}$, $B(t)=1200e^{0.01t}$. Meeting $t^*=\ln(B_0/A_0)/(k_A-k_B)\approx13.5155$. At $t=50$: $\ln(A/B)\approx1.0945$. Doubling clock of $A$ is $\ln 2/k_A\approx17.3287$.

tasks.title: Table — recover force, then doubling and threshold comparisons
tasks.context: A continuous exponential path $y(t)=y_0 e^{kt}$ is observed at two times (table). Recover the force by logarithm, then judge the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The doubling time is strictly less than $12$.
Fifteen years after $t=1$, the level strictly exceeds $2\,y(1)$.
The recovered force is strictly larger than $0.08$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Start from $y_2=y_1 e^{k\Delta t}$ and solve for $k$.

$$k=\frac{\ln(y_2/y_1)}{\Delta t}=\frac{\ln\!\bigl(y(6)/y(1)\bigr)}{5}$$

$$k=0.069315$$

The log-ratio formula is exactly the recovered force.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Doubling solves $e^{kt}=2$.

$$t_{\times 2}=\frac{\ln 2}{k}=10$$

$$10<12$$

Doubling finishes before twelve time units.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Propagate fifteen years from the first observation.

$$y(t_1+15)=y_1 e^{15k}\approx2262.7417$$

$$2y_1=1600$$

Fifteen years push the level past a double.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Evaluate the log-ratio between the tabulated points.

$$\ln(y_2/y_1)=k\cdot\Delta t=0.346574$$

$$0.346574>0.3$$

The log-ratio clears the $0.3$ threshold.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Compare the recovered force with $0.08$.

$$k=0.069315<0.08$$

The force equals $\ln 2/10\approx 0.0693$, below $0.08$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: From the table, $k=\ln(y_2/y_1)/\Delta t=0.069315$. Doubling $t_{\times 2}=10$; fifteen years after $t_1$: $y\approx2262.7417$; $\ln(y_2/y_1)=0.346574$.

tasks.title: Symbolic — nested exp∘log inverses of a continuous growth map
tasks.context: Let $f(t)=P e^{kt}$ with $P=250>0$ and $k=0.05>0$, and let $g$ be the inverse of $f$ on the range of $f$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Invert $y=P e^{kt}$ by taking logs.

$$g(y)=\frac{1}{k}\ln(y/P)$$

$$g(f(t))=\frac{1}{k}\ln(e^{kt})=t$$

Left-inverse holds on the whole real line.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Compose the other way on the positive reals.

$$f(g(y))=P\exp\bigl(\ln(y/P)\bigr)=y$$

Right-inverse holds for every $y>0$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Substitute the nested argument $P e^{2}$.

$$g(P e^{2})=\frac{1}{k}\ln(e^{2})=\frac{2}{k}$$

The nested exponential cancels under the log inverse.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Associativity of composition with a two-sided inverse.

$$(f\circ g\circ f)(t)=f\bigl(g(f(t))\bigr)=f(t)$$

The middle $g\circ f$ is the identity on the domain of $f$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Differentiate $k g(y)=\ln(y/P)$.

$$k g(y)=\ln y-\ln P$$

$$\frac{d}{dy}(k g(y))=\frac{1}{y}$$

The scaled inverse differentiates to the reciprocal.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview: $f(t)=P e^{kt}$ with $P=250$, $k=0.05$; inverse $g(y)=\frac{1}{k}\ln(y/P)$ on $(0,\infty)$. Nested check: $g(P e^{2})=2/k=40$.

tasks.title: Parametric — one surviving doubling claim in a force family
tasks.context: For each $a>0$ define $y_a(t)=a e^{kt}$ with fixed force $k=0.025$. Let $t_{\times 2}=\ln 2/k$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: For fixed $t>0$, the level $y_a(t)$ is maximised at $a=1/k$.
$\ln y_a(t)-\ln y_1(t)=\ln a+kt$ for every $a>0$ and every $t$.
The doubling time $t_{\times 2}$ depends on the parameter $a$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Every path doubles at the same clock, including $a=e^{2}$.

$$y_{e^{2}}(t_{\times 2})=e^{2}e^{k\cdot(\ln 2/k)}=e^{2}\cdot 2=2e^{2}$$

The nested exponential cancels and leaves a double.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Evaluate the claimed power identity.

$$y_a(1/k)=a e^{k\cdot(1/k)}=a e$$

$$a e\neq a^{e}\quad(a\neq e)$$

The path yields $ae$, not $a^{e}$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

At fixed $t$, $y_a(t)=a e^{kt}$ is strictly increasing in $a>0$.

$$\partial_a y_a(t)=e^{kt}>0$$

There is no maximiser at $a=1/k$ on $(0,\infty)$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Subtract log-levels carefully.

$$\ln y_a(t)-\ln y_1(t)=\ln a+kt-\ln 1-kt=\ln a$$

The $kt$ terms cancel; the claim keeps a spurious $+kt$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Doubling solves $e^{kt}=2$, independent of $a$.

$$t_{\times 2}=\frac{\ln 2}{k}=27.7259$$

The doubling clock does not depend on $a$.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Family $y_a(t)=a e^{0.025t}$. At $t=\ln 2/k=27.7259$, every path doubles its own $a$; in particular $y_{e^2}(27.7259)=2e^2$. Doubling time is independent of $a$.

tasks.title: Piecewise — continuity, log-increment, and average-force tests
tasks.context: A fund starts at $P_0=600$, grows at force $k_1=0.05$ on $[0,8]$, then at force $k_2=0.02$. Read the path at $t=20$ (figure). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The path is continuous at the switch $t=8$.
The late force $k_2$ strictly exceeds the path-average force $\bar k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Left and right limits share the matching factor $e^{k_1 T}$.

$$f(T^{-})=P_0 e^{k_1 T},\qquad f(T^{+})=P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2\cdot 0}$$

Both sides agree, so the path is continuous at the switch.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Logs add across the kink.

$$f(t)=P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)}$$

$$\ln(f(t)/P_0)=k_1 T+k_2(t-T)=0.64$$

The log-increment formula is exact.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Average force is log-increment over elapsed time.

$$\bar k=\frac{0.64}{20}=0.032>0.03$$

The average clears the $0.03$ threshold.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Compare the level with $3P_0$.

$$f(t)=P_0 e^{0.64}\approx1137.8885$$

$$3P_0=1800$$

The fund is still below three times its start.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Compare $k_2$ with the path average.

$$k_2=0.02,\qquad \bar k=0.032$$

$$0.02<0.032$$

The late force sits below the path average.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Switch at $T=8$: $f(T)\approx895.0948$. At $t=20$, $\ln(f/P_0)=0.64$ so $\bar k=0.032$. Compare $3P_0=1800$ with $f(t)\approx1137.8885$; late force $k_2=0.02<\bar k$.

tasks.title: Nested — exp∘log / log∘exp mashup beside a growth clock
tasks.context: Work with nested exponential and logarithmic compositions, and with the side path $P(t)=100 e^{0.02 t}$ (figure). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Change-of-base style nest: $\exp(c\ln a)=a^{c}$.

$$\exp(\ln 8/3)=8^{1/3}=2$$

The nest collapses to the cube root of eight.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Log-increment of the side path is force times time.

$$\ln(P(50)/100)=0.02\cdot 50=1$$

Fifty years at force $0.02$ produce log-increment $1$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Expand the quotient of exponentials.

$$\ln(e^{5}/e^{2})=5-2=3\neq 5/2$$

The nest yields $3$, not $5/2$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Inner $\exp\circ\ln$ cancels before the outer base-$2$ log.

$$\log_2(\exp(\ln 8))=\log_2 8=3$$

$$3\neq\ln 8$$

The value is $3$, not $\ln 8$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Peel the nest from the inside.

$$\ln e^{e}=e,\qquad \ln(\ln e^{e})=\ln e=1$$

$$\exp(1)=e\neq e^{2}$$

The nest equals $e$, not $e^{2}$.

So the statement is False.

tasks.title: Text-dense — continuous vs discrete clocks and a change-of-base identity
tasks.context: A principal $P=1000$ may grow continuously at force $k=0.04$ or discretely by factor $(1+r)$ each year with $r=0.04$. Let $t_d$ be continuous doubling time and $t_n$ discrete doubling time. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: At time $t_n$, the continuous path already strictly exceeds $2P$.
The discrete path reaches $2P$ at time $t=\ln 2/k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write both doubling clocks.

$$t_d=\frac{\ln 2}{k}\approx17.3287,\qquad t_n=\frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+r)}\approx17.673$$

$$17.3287<17.673$$

Continuous doubling finishes first.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Compare force with the discrete log-step.

$$\ln(1+r)=\ln(1.04)\approx0.039221$$

$$k=0.04>0.039221$$

Continuous force exceeds the discrete log-step.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Evaluate the continuous path at the discrete doubling clock.

$$P e^{k t_n}=P\exp\!\bigl(k\ln 2/\ln(1+r)\bigr)\approx2027.7352$$

$$2027.7352>2P=2000$$

Continuous growth has already cleared a double by $t_n$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Change of base on an exponential.

$$\log_2(e^{kt})=\frac{\ln(e^{kt})}{\ln 2}=\frac{kt}{\ln 2}$$

The change-of-base identity holds for every $t$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Discrete doubling uses $\ln(1+r)$, not $k$.

$$\frac{\ln 2}{k}\approx17.3287\neq t_n\approx17.673$$

The continuous doubling clock is not the discrete hitting time.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Continuous doubling $t_d=\ln 2/k\approx17.3287$; discrete $t_n=\ln 2/\ln(1+r)\approx17.673$. Since $k>\ln(1+r)$, continuous leads; at $t_n$ continuous level $\approx2027.7352$.

tasks.title: Rebuild — three consistent samples force a unique continuous $k$
tasks.context: A continuous exponential path is observed at three times (table). Rebuild pairwise forces and compare. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Those two adjacent rebuilt forces are equal.

**C.** → True

$$k_{01}=0.03=k_{12}$$

Equal adjacent forces certify a single continuous $k$.

**D.** → True

Outer rebuild agrees with the adjacent ones.

tasks.title: Applied letters — GDP per-capita force with four tempting misreads
tasks.context: GDP follows $Y(t)=Y_0 e^{gt}$ and population $N(t)=N_0 e^{pt}$ with $Y_0=200$, $g=0.04$, $N_0=10$, $p=0.01$. Per-capita output is $y=Y/N$. Horizon $t=25$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Per-capita output doubles on or before $t=20$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Per-capita log-derivative is the difference of forces.

$$\frac{d}{dt}\ln y=g-p$$

The per-capita force is exactly $g-p$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$\Delta\ln y=(g-p)t=0.75\neq g t=1$$

Population force must be subtracted.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$y(t)/y(0)=e^{(g-p)t}=e^{0.75}\neq e^{gt}$$

The exponent is $k=g-p$, not $g$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$\Delta\ln Y-\Delta\ln N=gt-pt=(g-p)$$

$$g-p=0.03\neq g+p=0.05$$

Differences of log-increments give $g-p$, not $g+p$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

$$y(20)/y(0)=e^{20k}=e^{0.6}\approx1.8221$$

$$<2$$

At $t=20$ per-capita output has not yet doubled.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Per-capita force $k=g-p=0.03$. Over $t=25$, $\Delta\ln y=0.75$. Doubling needs $\ln 2/k\approx23.1049$; at $t=20$ the per-capita factor is only $e^{0.6}$.

tasks.title: Hybrid — piecewise stock force beside constant-elasticity demand
tasks.context: A stock starts at $P_0=1000$, grows at force $k_1=0.06$ until $t=5$, then at force $k_2=0.02$. Separately prices drift at force $g=0.04$ with demand elasticity magnitude $b=1.5$. Read the stock at horizon $t=15$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The average stock force $\bar k=\ln(f(15)/P_0)/15$ exceeds $0.03$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$f(t)=P_0 e^{k_1 T}e^{k_2(t-T)}$$

$$\ln(f(t)/P_0)=0.5$$

Logs add across the kink.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$\bar k=0.033333>0.03$$

Path-average force clears $0.03$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$\frac{d\ln Q}{dt}=-bg=-0.06$$

Constant elasticity converts price force into quantity force.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

$$b=1.5>1$$

Demand is elastic, not inelastic.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

$$f(t)\approx1648.7213<2P_0=2000$$

The stock has not yet doubled.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Log-increment $0.5$, $\bar k=0.033333$. Quantity force $-bg=-0.06$. At $t=15$, $f\approx1648.7213$ vs $2P_0=2000$.

tasks.title: Graph — decaying mass versus growing fund and the meeting clock
tasks.context: A mass $M(t)=M_0 e^{-k_d t}$ with $M_0=2000$, $k_d=0.05$ competes with a fund $P(t)=P_0 e^{k_g t}$ with $P_0=500$, $k_g=0.03$. The figure shows both on $[0,40]$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The two paths meet at some time strictly inside $(0,40)$.
At $t=40$, the fund strictly exceeds the mass.
The half-life of the mass equals $\ln 2/k_d$.
The meeting time equals the half-life of the mass.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$t^*=\frac{\ln(M_0/P_0)}{k_g+k_d}\approx17.3287$$

$$0<17.3287<40$$

A unique crossing sits inside the window.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$P(40)\approx1660.0585,\qquad M(40)\approx270.6706$$

The fund leads at the horizon.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Set $M_0 e^{-k_d t}=P_0 e^{k_g t}$ and take logs.

$$t^*=\frac{\ln(M_0/P_0)}{k_g+k_d}$$

Opposite-sign forces add in the denominator.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln 2}{k_d}=13.8629$$

Half-life is the standard log-two clock.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

$$t^*\approx17.3287\neq t_{1/2}=13.8629$$

Meeting and half-life are different clocks.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Mass $M(t)=2000e^{-0.05t}$, fund $P(t)=500e^{0.03t}$. Meeting $t^*=\ln(M_0/P_0)/(k_g+k_d)\approx17.3287$. Half-life $\ln 2/k_d\approx13.8629$.

tasks.title: Table — recover two forces, then judge the future crossing
tasks.context: Two continuous exponential series $A$ and $B$ are sampled at $t=0$ and $t=5$ (table). Recover forces, then judge the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The recovered force of $B$ strictly exceeds that of $A$.
The series have already met on $[0,5]$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$k_A=\frac{\ln(A(5)/A(0))}{5}=0.05$$

Log recovery returns force $0.05$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

$$k_B=0.02<0.05=k_A$$

Force $B$ is smaller, not larger.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

$$t^*=\frac{\ln(B_0/A_0)}{k_A-k_B}\approx18.6539>5$$

The crossing lies after the observation window.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$\frac{\ln(A_0/B_0)}{k_A-k_B}\approx-18.6539<0$$

Flipping the ratio makes the formula negative.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

$$A(5)\approx513.61<B(5)\approx773.62$$

At the second observation $B$ is still larger.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Recovered $k_A=0.05$, $k_B=0.02$. Crossing $t^*\approx18.6539>=5$. At observation, $A\approx513.61<B\approx773.62$.

tasks.title: Symbolic — change-of-base inequalities and product/power traps
tasks.context: Compare logarithms at different bases and test standard log identities. The figure shows $y=\log_2 x$ for reference. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Change of base: $\log_b 12=\ln 12/\ln b$, decreasing in $b>1$.

$$\log_2 12\approx3.585>\log_3 12\approx2.2619$$

Smaller base yields a larger logarithm of the same argument.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$\log_2 12=\frac{\ln 12}{\ln 2}$$

Change-of-base is an identity.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

$$\log_2 12+\log_2 3=\log_2(12\cdot 3)=\log_2 36\neq\log_2 15$$

The product rule produces $\log_2 36$, not $\log_2 15$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$\log_5(1/25)=\log_5(5^{-2})=-2\neq 2$$

The power is negative two.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

$$\frac{\ln 9}{\ln 3}=\log_3 9=2\not>3$$

The change-of-base quotient equals $2$, not more than $3$.

So the statement is False.

tasks.title: Parametric — unit-start exponential locked to a doubling clock of $5$
tasks.context: Let $y(t)=e^{kt}$ with the force fixed by the normalisation $y(5)=2$ (equivalently $k=\ln 2/5$). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
tactical_explanations:

$$y(5)=e^{k\cdot 5}=e^{\ln 2}=2$$

The normalisation forces $y(5)=2$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$y(10)=e^{2\ln 2}=4$$

Ten units are two doubling clocks.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$\frac{\ln y(15)}{15}=\frac{15k}{15}=k$$

Log-level over time recovers the force.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$y(t)^{2}=e^{2kt}=e^{k(2t)}=y(2t)$$

Squaring the level doubles the clock.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$t_{\times 2}=\frac{\ln 2}{k}=5$$

Doubling time is exactly five.

So the statement is True.

$$Y(T)=Y_0 e^{g_1 T}=164.8721$$

and the late segment starts from that same level.

Matching levels make GDP continuous at the switch.

$$\Delta\ln Y=g_1 T+g_2(t-T)=0.7$$

Piecewise GDP logs add.

tasks.title: Nested — log constraint on force beside an inverse evaluation
tasks.context: A growth map $f(t)=P e^{kt}$ is constrained by the nested-log link $\ln(k/0.01)=\ln 3$ and by $P=e^{2}$. Let $g$ be the inverse of $f$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $f$ doubles its initial level in time $\ln 2/k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\ln(k/0.01)=\ln 3\implies k/0.01=3\implies k=0.03$$

The nested log link collapses to $k=0.03$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$f(\ln 2/k)=P e^{\ln 2}=2P$$

The standard doubling clock works under the constrained force.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

$$\ln P=\ln(e^{2})=2$$

The initial level is exactly $e^{2}$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

$$k/0.01=3\neq e^{3}$$

The link gives ratio $3$, not $e^{3}$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

$$g(e)=\frac{1}{k}\ln(e/P)=\frac{1-2}{k}=-33.3333$$

$$-33.3333\neq 1/k$$

Because $P=e^{2}>e$, the inverse at $e$ is negative.

So the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview: Constraint $\ln(k/0.01)=\ln 3$ forces $k=0.03$. $P=e^{2}$ so $\ln P=2$. Doubling clock $t=\ln 2/k\approx23.1049$. Inverse $g(e)=(1/k)\ln(e/P)=-33.3333$.

tasks.title: Text-dense — five mixed exp/log micro-claims, one survivor

The power is negative three.

So the statement is False.

Sixteen is $2^4$, not $2^8$.

So the statement is False.

The nest yields nine.

So the statement is False.

tasks.title: Rebuild — semi-log sample slopes versus discrete and linear traps
tasks.context: A continuous exponential is sampled at three times (table). The figure shows the semi-log path. Rebuild slopes from the samples. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The semi-log slope between $t=0$ and $t=10$ equals $k=0.04$.
The semi-log slope between $t=0$ and $t=5$ equals $k=0.04$.
The discrete path $P_0(1+0.04)^{t}$ shares the same semi-log slope $k$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

$$\frac{\ln y(10)-\ln y(0)}{10}=0.04$$

Outer semi-log slope recovers $k$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

$$\frac{\ln y(5)-\ln y(0)}{5}=0.04$$

Adjacent semi-log slope recovers the same $k$.

**C.** → False

$$\ln\bigl(P_0(1+k)^{t}\bigr)=\ln P_0+t\ln(1+k)$$

$$\ln(1+k)\approx0.039221\neq k$$

Discrete semi-log slope is $\ln(1+k)$, not $k$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

$$\frac{y(10)}{y(0)}=e^{0.4}\approx1.4918$$

$$1+10k=1.4$$

Linearisation $1+kt$ is not the exponential ratio.
